ch06 - Introduction Warm-Up.md
chapters.relation: Andy Wible's introduction argues that if Plato and Aristotle were alive they would be avid golfers, because both golf and philosophy seduce great minds with problems that look easy yet prove endlessly difficult. It frames golf as 'a Sudoku that cannot be solved' and pairs it with the eternal questions (right and wrong, who am I, beauty, God, meaning) to preview the volume's chapters. Golf becomes a vehicle for the examined life, enlivening philosophy through the lived experience of the game.

chapters.file: ch07 - The Front Nine.md
ch08 - I. The Beauty of the Game.md
ch09 - First Hole Golf and the Importance of Play.md
chapters.relation: Al Gini defends play as intrinsically valuable and essential to being human, drawing on Huizinga's three criteria of 'true play' and William James's ideal of the amateur who plays 'for the love of it.' Using his golf-obsessed father as an extended case, he shows how golf functions as a self-contained, absorbing 'refuge from ordinary life' that delivers completion, coordination, and cooperation, echoing Plato's claim in the Republic and Laws that sport forms both person and community. The chapter treats golf as an end in itself whose joy sustains a flourishing life rather than as a means to external reward.

chapters.file: ch10 - Second Hole On the Beauty and Sublimity of Golf.md
chapters.relation: Fudge and Ulatowski argue that golf's aesthetic appeal has two sources: the course as a designed landscape best appreciated (via Walton's 'Categories of Art') under the category of gardens, and the sublimity of players' character. They apply Kant's 'Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime' to distinguish beautiful courses (Augusta) from sublime ones (Pebble Beach, St. Andrews) and to explain Bobby Jones's self-imposed penalty at the 1925 U.S. Open as the noble sublime, since 'subduing one's passions through principles is sublime.' They link the consistent rule-following golf demands to Kant's categorical imperative and read human dignity as 'beyond price' against Hobbes's price-based account, while Schopenhauer's critique of the French garden frames the environmental objection to courses.

chapters.file: ch11 - II. Golf and Moral Character.md
ch12 - Third Hole Finding the (Fair)Way with Confucius and Ben Hogan.md
chapters.relation: Laumakis builds an analogy between pursuing excellence in golf and living a flourishing human life, then contrasts two models. Reading Confucius's Great Learning and Analects onto golf, he casts a repeating swing as a 'well-ordered kingdom' rooted in self-cultivation, and reinterprets ren, li, yi, and xiao so the 'authoritative player' masters the game through ritual practice, a teacher-parent (xiao), and doing what is appropriate in each lie. Against this social conception he sets Ben Hogan's Five Lessons as a 'rugged individualist' account stressing solitary practice and personal responsibility, and proposes a contextual pluralism as a mean between communitarian absolutism and individualist relativism.

chapters.file: ch13 - Fourth Hole “Quiet…Please!” Reflections on Golf and Civility.md
chapters.relation: McNaron argues that golf promotes civility both empirically and normatively through its rules (self-scoring, self-called penalties) and its etiquette (silence during a swing, care for the course). Using an Aristotelian virtue-ethics frame plus Kekes's 'conduct according to custom' and Calhoun's expressivist account of civility as communicating respect, he treats civility as a mean acquired by habituation and opposes it to skloka, the petty hostility of win-at-all-costs sport. He defends golf's quiet against charges of classism, reads Tiger Woods's outburst at a shutter-clicking photographer as justified anger at an etiquette breach, and names the Ryder Cup's jingoism, boorish spectators, and intrusive media as threats to golf's civil, contemplative character.

chapters.file: ch14 - Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character.md
chapters.relation: Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.

chapters.file: ch15 - Sixth Hole Virtue Ethics From Caddyshack to Better Golf.md
chapters.relation: McElreath tests three ethical theories against golf intuitions and argues virtue ethics wins. Consequentialism rightly judges a postal carrier's choice to work over golf but wrongly permits Judge Smails in Caddyshack to kick his ball when no bad consequences follow; Kantian ethics correctly condemns Smails's deceptive maxim as non-universalizable but mishandles the play-versus-work case. Virtue ethics, judging acts by what an ideally virtuous person would characteristically do, gets both right via the relevant virtues of justice and honesty, and he then applies benevolence, justice, and tolerance to argue golf should better treat women, minorities, disabled players (Casey Martin's cart), and homosexuals.

chapters.file: ch16 - III. Ethical Issues within Golf.md
ch17 - Seventh Hole Cheating and Gamesmanship among Amateur and Professional Golfers.md
chapters.relation: Lumpkin argues that amateur golfers routinely cheat while professionals do not, and dissects four rationalizations amateurs use: appeal to ignorance, appeal to popularity, appeal to tradition (Callahan's 'cheating culture'), and the belief that 'no one will ever know' — a golf-course version of Plato's Ring of Gyges where invisibility dissolves restraint. Drawing on Kohlberg's stages of moral development, she claims professionals reason at higher levels because officials, peers, and disqualification (e.g., J. P. Hayes) enforce the sport's social contract, whereas amateurs face no punishment. She concludes casual golfers would do better not to keep score than to keep a 'mythical' one, earning the right to score only once they follow the rules.

chapters.file: ch18 - Eighth Hole Playing Through Racism and Sexism in Golf.md
chapters.relation: Gray examines whether golf is a model of equality or a preserve of 'wealthy white men,' using George Carlin's polemic and the Tiger Woods 'Chosen One' narrative as foils. He documents 'social closure' and the 'Grass Ceiling' through Augusta National's history, the Shoal Creek and Martha Burk/NCWO controversies, and the PGA's former Caucasian-only clause, then turns to sexism via McGinnis, McQuillan, and Chapple's interviews and Connell's 'hegemonic masculinity,' showing how gendered 'red/women's tees' entrench a false dualism of male and female play. Citing McDonagh and Pappano's Playing with the Boys, he argues coercive sex-segregation rests on false assumptions and calls for transparency about club membership.

chapters.file: ch19 - IV. Golf and Rationality.md
ch20 - Ninth Hole Is Golf Inherently Irrational.md
chapters.relation: Shier asks why it is not insane to deliberately place obstacles (rules, hazards) between oneself and one's goal, quoting Woodrow Wilson and Mike Seabrook on golf's 'essential lunacy.' He distinguishes internal goals (holing the ball in fewest strokes) from external goals (challenge, competition, fresh air) and, echoing Aristotle, argues excellent conditions lie at the mean between too-hard and too-easy: the regulatory and environmental restrictions make internal goals difficult precisely so external goals become achievable, so the obstacles are rational, not irrational. Using Bernard Suits's view of games as 'the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles,' he applies the framework to handicapping, ad hoc anti-Tiger course changes, and distance technology that threatens golf's characteristic skill set.

holes.name: Philosophy of Play
holes.what: The view, developed by Huizinga and Diane Ackerman among others, that play is a free, self-contained, intrinsically valuable activity outside ordinary utility that is constitutive of being human.
holes.why: Chapter 9 is centrally about play as an end in itself (Huizinga's three criteria, 'true play') and no existing taxonomy concept names play as such rather than eudaimonia or meaning.

holes.name: Game-Playing as Voluntary Overcoming of Unnecessary Obstacles
holes.what: Bernard Suits's definition of game-playing as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles, distinguishing pre-lusory goals from the lusory attitude that accepts constitutive rules.
holes.why: Chapter 20's whole argument is built on Suits's account (internal vs. external goals mirror his pre-lusory/lusory distinction), and the taxonomy has no concept or philosopher for the philosophy of games/sport.
